item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.content:encoded:
Active Medical Conditions

Primary Diagnosis

Stage IV (Metastatic) Colorectal Adenocarcinoma

  • Diagnosed: November 8, 2023
  • Grade: Grade 2 (moderately differentiated)
  • Primary Site: Colon
  • Metastatic Sites: Liver (multiple, bilobar)
  • Genomic Profile:
    • MSS (Microsatellite Stable)
    • KRAS wild-type
    • TP53 mutated
  • Performance Status: ECOG 0-1
  • Status: Active, on systemic chemotherapy

Secondary Conditions

Hypertension

  • Onset: ~2010
  • Management: Antihypertensive medications
  • Stability: Well-controlled

Hyperlipidemia

  • Onset: ~2012
  • Management: Statin therapy
  • Stability: Well-controlled

Obesity

  • BMI Category: Overweight to Obese range
  • Status: Ongoing management

Treatment-Related Conditions

Chemotherapy Side Effects (Ongoing)

  • Peripheral neuropathy (FOLFIRI-related)
  • Occasional nausea/vomiting
  • Fatigue
  • Hand-foot syndrome (potential with Bevacizumab)

Port Placement

  • Central venous port for chemotherapy administration
  • Status: Active, functioning

Allergies

  • No known drug allergies (NKDA)
  • No known food allergies

See Active Medications for current treatment regimen.

item.title: Current Medications
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: Active medication regimen and treatment protocols
item.content:encoded:
Active Medication Regimen

Chemotherapy Protocol: FOLFIRI + Bevacizumab

Protocol Name: 5-FU/Leucovorin/Irinotecan (FOLFIRI) + Bevacizumab (Avastin)

Indication: Stage IV metastatic colorectal cancer with liver metastases

Cycle: 14 days (biweekly)

Components

  1. Bevacizumab (Avastin)

    • Dose: 5 mg/kg IV
    • Frequency: Day 1 of each cycle
    • Route: Intravenous infusion
    • Mechanism: VEGF inhibitor (angiogenesis inhibitor)

  2. Irinotecan (Camptosar)

    • Dose: 180 mg/m² IV
    • Frequency: Day 1 of each cycle
    • Route: Intravenous infusion
    • Mechanism: Topoisomerase I inhibitor

  3. Leucovorin (Folinic Acid)

    • Dose: 400 mg/m² IV
    • Frequency: Day 1 of each cycle
    • Route: Intravenous infusion
    • Purpose: Potentiates 5-fluorouracil

  4. 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU)

    • Dose: 400 mg/m² IV bolus + 2400 mg/m² continuous infusion
    • Frequency: Day 1 (bolus), Days 1-2 (continuous infusion)
    • Route: Intravenous
    • Mechanism: Antimetabolite chemotherapy

Supportive Medications

Antiemetics

  • Ondansetron (Zofran) — 5-HT3 antagonist for nausea/vomiting
  • Dexamethasone — Corticosteroid for nausea prophylaxis
  • Aprepitant (Emend) — NK1 antagonist for breakthrough nausea

Anti-diarrheal

  • Loperamide (Imodium) — For chemotherapy-induced diarrhea

Neuropathy Management

  • Gabapentin — For peripheral neuropathy

Chronic Medications (Non-chemotherapy)

Cardiovascular

  • Antihypertensive agent — Blood pressure management
  • Statin — Lipid management

Other

  • Multivitamin with minerals — Nutritional supplementation

Monitoring Parameters

  • CBC with differential — Before each chemotherapy cycle
  • CMP (metabolic panel) — Before each cycle and periodically
  • LFTs (liver function tests) — Regular monitoring given liver involvement
  • CEA level — Tumor marker monitoring
  • Imaging (CT) — Every 2-3 months for response assessment

Side Effect Management

See Active Conditions for treatment-related conditions and management strategies.

Last Updated: February 2025

Note: This is a personal documentation of medications and should not be used for medical decision-making. Always consult with healthcare providers regarding medication management.

item.title: Data Sources & Documentation
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: Documentation of medical record sources and data provenance
item.content:encoded:
Medical Record Sources

This section documents the sources of medical records in this repository and data collection methodologies.

Primary Data Sources

Epic Electronic Health Record (EHR)

  • Facility: Anderson Cancer Center (UTMDACC), Houston, TX
  • Data Access: Patient portal export (CCDA XML format)
  • Frequency: Periodic exports (approximately monthly)
  • Content: Encounters, medications, labs, vital signs, clinical notes, imaging reports

MediTech EHR

  • Facility: SIHF hospital system
  • Data Access: Paper records transcribed and digitized
  • Frequency: As-needed when records needed
  • Content: Inpatient encounters, nursing notes, provider documentation

Athena EHR

  • Facility: Specialty clinics
  • Data Access: Patient portal and direct export
  • Frequency: When updates available
  • Content: Outpatient visits, consultations, test results

Secondary Data Sources

Laboratory Reports

  • Source: Direct from lab portals (LabCorp, Quest, hospital labs)
  • Format: PDF reports or portal display
  • Content: Lab values, reference ranges, trending data

Imaging Studies

  • Source: DICOM viewers, radiology report PDFs
  • Format: PDF radiologist reports + DICOM metadata
  • Content: Imaging findings, impression, clinical correlation

Pathology Reports

  • Source: Hospital pathology department
  • Format: PDF pathology reports
  • Content: Specimen description, microscopic findings, diagnosis

Data Preservation & Privacy

De-identification

  • Patient ID numbers replaced with generic identifiers
  • Facility names may be generalized or abbreviated
  • Specific provider names may be removed or anonymized
  • Medical record numbers and encounter IDs removed

Retention

  • Data preserved in this repository for personal archival
  • Shared publicly to facilitate research and patient advocacy
  • No sensitive identifiers retained
  • HIPAA-compliant handling

Data Format & Organization

Directory Structure

medical/
├── encounters/    # Structured encounter data
├── labs/         # Lab results with trending
├── imaging/      # Radiology reports
├── pathology/    # Pathology reports
├── surgical/     # Operative reports
├── notes/        # Clinical notes
└── analysis/     # Synthesized clinical analysis

File Formats

  • Markdown (.md) — Primary format for all medical documents
  • Metadata: YAML front matter with standardized fields
  • Structured Data: Tables for labs, encounters, medications
  • Charts: Chart.js for laboratory trending

Data Quality & Curation

Manual Review

  • Each document reviewed for accuracy and de-identification
  • Cross-referenced with primary sources
  • Dates and timelines verified
  • Lab values double-checked against portals

Standardization

  • Standardized date formats (YYYY-MM-DD)
  • Consistent units and reference ranges cited
  • Medical terminology standardized
  • Abbreviations documented

External References

Clinical Protocols

  • NCCN Guidelines for Colorectal Cancer
  • ASCO Treatment Recommendations
  • Published literature on FOLFIRI + Bevacizumab

Research Data

  • Clinical trial protocols (where applicable)
  • Treatment outcome data
  • Prognostic marker information

Data Limitations

  1. Incomplete Records — Some early records may be unavailable
  2. Transcription Accuracy — Paper records transcribed manually may contain errors
  3. Temporal Gaps — Some encounters may have incomplete documentation
  4. Provider Variation — Different providers document using different templates
  5. Lab Reference Ranges — May vary between facilities and testing methods

Access & Citation

These medical records are provided as a public health resource. If citing specific data from this repository, please reference:

Medical Records Archive. https://metafunctor.com/medical/

For specific documents, include the date and type of record.

Contact & Feedback

Questions about data sources, accuracy, or privacy concerns can be directed to the main site contact information.

Last Updated: February 2025

item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: Radiological studies including CT, MRI, and other imaging
item.content:encoded:
Imaging Reports

This section contains radiological reports and diagnostic imaging studies.

Imaging Types

CT (Computed Tomography)

  • CT Chest — Thoracic imaging
  • CT Abdomen/Pelvis — Abdominal and pelvic organs
  • Diagnostic CT — Staging and surveillance
  • CT with IV contrast — Enhanced visualization

MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging)

  • Brain MRI — Neuroimaging
  • Liver MRI — Hepatic lesion characterization

Ultrasound

  • Abdominal ultrasound — Hepatic and abdominal assessment
  • Vascular studies — Venous and arterial evaluation

Other Imaging

  • PET/CT — Positron emission tomography for metastatic disease
  • Bone scan — Skeletal metastasis assessment

Staging & Surveillance

Initial imaging for cancer staging established baseline disease extent. Surveillance imaging every 2-3 months monitors:

  • Response to chemotherapy
  • Progression or regression of metastases
  • Development of new lesions
  • Treatment effect on known lesions

Report Format

Each imaging report includes:

  • Study Type — What was imaged
  • Date — Study date
  • Technique — Imaging parameters
  • Findings — Detailed description of organs and lesions
  • Impression — Summary and clinical correlation
  • Comparison — To prior studies

Individual imaging reports are filed chronologically.

Overview

This section contains my comprehensive medical records and health dashboard, documenting my cancer diagnosis journey, treatment protocols, clinical encounters, lab results, imaging studies, and pathology reports.

Last Updated: February 2025

Quick Navigation

  • Clinical Timeline — Chronological view of all medical events
  • Lab Results & Trends — Laboratory values with interactive charts
  • Active Conditions — Current diagnoses and comorbidities
  • Medications — Current medication regimen
  • Clinical Encounters — Hospital visits and appointments
  • Imaging Reports — CT scans, MRI, and other imaging studies
  • Pathology Reports — Biopsy and tissue analysis
  • Surgical Procedures — Surgical interventions and timelines
  • Clinical Notes — Provider notes and assessments
  • Analysis & Research — Clinical analysis and research documents
  • Data Sources — Documentation of data collection and sources

Purpose

This public medical records repository serves several purposes:

  • Transparency — Documenting my health journey openly
  • Research — Contributing to medical research and understanding of cancer treatment protocols
  • Community — Helping others navigating similar diagnoses and treatment decisions
  • Personal Archive — Comprehensive historical record of medical encounters and outcomes

Data Privacy

All medical records are shared publicly with de-identification applied where appropriate. No genetic data, detailed provider identifiable information, or sensitive social determinants are included.

Diagnosis

Stage IV (Metastatic) Colorectal Cancer diagnosed November 2023

  • Sites: Liver metastases (multiple, bilobar)
  • Grade: Grade 2 (moderately differentiated)
  • Genetic Profile: MSS (microsatellite stable), wild-type KRAS
  • Ongoing Treatment: Systemic chemotherapy with FOLFIRI + Bevacizumab protocol

Contact & Questions

For questions about medical content or collaboration opportunities, see the main site contact information.

Disclaimer: This is a personal medical record repository intended for patient documentation and educational purposes. Content is not a substitute for professional medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment.

item.title: Pathology Reports
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.content:encoded:
Pathology Reports

This section contains pathology reports from tissue biopsies and specimen analysis.

Report Components

Each pathology report includes:

  • Specimen Type — What tissue was examined
  • Clinical History — Indication for biopsy
  • Gross Description — What the tissue looked like to the naked eye
  • Microscopic Description — What was seen under the microscope
  • Immunohistochemistry — Special stains if performed
  • Molecular Studies — Genetic/molecular testing results
  • Diagnosis — Pathological interpretation
  • Comment — Clinical significance if applicable

Diagnostic Studies

Tumor Characterization

  • Tumor type (adenocarcinoma, etc.)
  • Grade (differentiation level)
  • Histological subtype
  • Special features

Genomic Profiling

  • Microsatellite instability (MSI) status
  • KRAS mutation status
  • BRAF mutation status
  • TP53 status
  • Mismatch repair gene status

Prognostic Markers

  • Ki-67 proliferation index
  • Lymphocytic infiltration
  • Vascular invasion
  • Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs)

Individual pathology reports are filed with associated specimen information.

item.title: Quick Start Guide
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: How to navigate and use the medical records section
item.content:encoded:
Medical Records - Quick Start Guide

Accessing the Medical Dashboard

Navigate to https://metafunctor.com/medical/ to access the medical records dashboard.

You can also reach it from:

  • Main site navigation menu (top “Medical” link)
  • The blog post: Stage 4: Almost a Year After the Defense

Understanding the Dashboard

The medical dashboard serves as a central index for all health documentation. It includes:

  • Overview — Cancer diagnosis context and treatment approach
  • Navigation shortcuts — Quick links to all subsections
  • Data privacy statement — How medical information is handled
  • Contact information — How to reach out with questions

Using the Sidebar Navigation

On every medical page, you’ll see a sidebar on the right side containing 11 navigation links:

  1. Dashboard — Return to the main overview
  2. Timeline — Chronological view of medical events
  3. Conditions — Active diagnoses (Stage IV colorectal cancer, etc.)
  4. Medications — Current treatment protocol and supporting drugs
  5. Encounters — Medical appointments and hospital visits
  6. Labs — Laboratory test results with trends
  7. Imaging — CT scans, MRI, and other radiological studies
  8. Pathology — Biopsy reports and tissue analysis
  9. Surgical — Surgical procedures and operative reports
  10. Notes — Clinical documentation and provider notes
  11. Analysis — Synthesized clinical analysis and research
  12. Sources — Documentation of data sources and methodology

Navigation Tips:

  • The current page link is highlighted in blue
  • Click any link to navigate to that section
  • The sidebar stays visible as you scroll
  • On mobile devices, the sidebar appears below the main content

Finding Information

If you’re looking for…

When did the cancer start? → See Timeline or Conditions

What’s the treatment plan? → See Medications

Lab value history and trends → See Labs

Imaging findings and reports → See Imaging

Provider notes and assessments → See Notes

Research or clinical analysis → See Analysis

How the data was collected → See Sources

Understanding the Information

Front Matter

Each medical record includes metadata at the top (not visible on the page):

  • Title — What the page is about
  • Date — When the medical event occurred
  • Categories — All pages are “medical” and “personal”
  • Tags — Specific keywords (e.g., “cancer”, “stage-4”, “labs”)

Content Format

Medical records use standardized formatting:

Tables — Lab results and encounter data are shown in tables with columns for:

  • Test name or Encounter type
  • Date — When the test/appointment occurred
  • Value — Result, reference range, or assessment
  • Status — Normal, abnormal, or clinical significance

Sections — Documents are divided into clear sections:

  • Overview or summary
  • Detailed findings or results
  • Clinical impression or assessment
  • Next steps or follow-up

Breadcrumbs — At the top of each page showing your location:

Home / Medical / [Current Section]

Searching for Information

Using Site Search

  1. Go to Search
  2. Type a keyword or phrase:
    • Medical terms: “CEA”, “creatinine”, “imaging”
    • Dates: “February 2025”, “January”
    • Topics: “chemotherapy”, “appointments”, “CT scan”
    • Medication names: “FOLFIRI”, “Bevacizumab”

Medical pages appear in search results with:

  • Title — The page name
  • Section — Will show “medical”
  • Content preview — First 500 characters

Filtering Search Results

After searching, you can filter by:

  • Section — Select “medical”
  • Tags — Select specific tags like “cancer” or “treatment”
  • Categories — Select “medical”

Understanding Medical Abbreviations

Common abbreviations used in medical records:

Diagnoses & Types

  • IV — Intravenous
  • CT — Computed Tomography
  • MRI — Magnetic Resonance Imaging
  • CEA — Carcinoembryonic antigen (tumor marker)

Lab Tests

  • CBC — Complete Blood Count
  • CMP — Comprehensive Metabolic Panel
  • LFTs — Liver Function Tests
  • AST/ALT — Liver enzymes

Medications

  • 5-FU — 5-Fluorouracil (chemotherapy)
  • FOLFIRI — Fluorouracil + Leucovorin + Irinotecan protocol
  • IV — Intravenous administration

See Sources for more detailed definitions and medical context.

Interpreting Results

Lab Values

Lab results show:

  1. Test name — What was measured
  2. Result — The actual value
  3. Reference range — Normal range for that test
  4. Status — Whether the value is normal or abnormal

Example:

| Test | Value | Reference | Status |
|------|-------|-----------|--------|
| Hemoglobin | 11.2 | 12.0-16.0 | Low |

The hemoglobin value (11.2) is below the normal range (12.0-16.0), so it’s marked as “Low”.

Imaging Reports

Imaging reports include:

  1. Study type — What was imaged (e.g., “CT Abdomen/Pelvis”)
  2. Date — When the study was performed
  3. Findings — Description of what was seen
  4. Impression — Clinical interpretation

Clinical Notes

Clinical notes follow a standard format:

  1. Date & provider — When and by whom
  2. Assessment — Clinical impression and problem list
  3. Plan — Treatment recommendations and next steps
  4. Follow-up — When to return, what to watch for

Privacy & De-identification

All medical records in this section:

  • Are publicly shared for educational and research purposes
  • Have removed identifiers (no patient ID numbers, specific provider names)
  • Use generalized facility names (not specific hospital identifiers)
  • Do not include genetic data or sensitive social information

See Sources for complete privacy information.

Navigating on Mobile

On mobile devices:

  1. Sidebar appears below content — Scroll down to see navigation
  2. Breadcrumb at top — Shows where you are
  3. Tap navigation links — Sidebar links are touch-friendly
  4. Tables may scroll — Wide tables scroll horizontally on small screens
  5. One-column layout — All content stacks vertically

Mobile navigation tip: Use the breadcrumb at the top to go back to “Medical” then select a new section.

Linking to Medical Content

To link from external sites or other sections of metafunctor to medical content, use:

[Medical Records](/medical/)
[My Treatment Protocol](/medical/medications/)
[Lab Results](/medical/labs/)

Getting Help

Common Questions

Q: Is all this information accurate? A: This information is transcribed from official medical records. While care is taken to maintain accuracy, it represents patient records and may contain transcription or formatting variations.

Q: Can I use this for medical advice? A: No. This is a personal medical record repository. Always consult healthcare providers for medical decisions.

Q: Can I share this information? A: Yes, this is publicly shared information. Attribution to metafunctor.com is appreciated.

Q: Are there gaps in the data? A: Yes. Some early records may be unavailable, and documentation may be incomplete for certain periods.

Contact

For questions or corrections about medical content, see the main site contact information.

Navigation Tips

  1. Bookmark /medical/ for quick access
  2. Use search for specific lab values or dates
  3. Follow breadcrumbs to navigate back to Medical section
  4. Start with dashboard for overview, then dive into subsections
  5. Check Timeline if you want chronological view of events

Next Steps

  • Return to Dashboard — Start here
  • Read About the Treatment — Learn about FOLFIRI protocol
  • View Lab Results — See lab trends
  • Explore Timeline — See chronological events
  • Search Medical Content — Find specific information

For more information: See Sources or the main README.

Last updated: February 2025
